words.definition: thinly scattered or distributed; meager
words.nuance: Neutral; it stresses thinness of distribution.
examples: The desert supports only sparse vegetation.
Evidence for the theory remains sparse.

words.definition: not to be relied on or trusted; possibly false
words.nuance: On the GRE, the adjective sense is common: suspect data or a suspect motive.
examples: The study's conclusions are suspect because of its tiny sample.
His sudden generosity seemed suspect to his rivals.

words.definition: too long, slow or dull; tiresome
words.nuance: Stresses boredom from length or monotony.
examples: Entering the data by hand was a tedious task.
The lecture grew tedious after the first hour.

words.definition: the state of being strong and active; energy
words.nuance: Positive; used of people, economies and cultures.
examples: The new market restored vitality to the old downtown.
Even at ninety she radiated vitality.

words.definition: playfully quaint or fanciful, especially in an appealing way; acting on whim
words.nuance: Usually affectionate, but can suggest unpredictability.
examples: The children's book is filled with whimsical illustrations.
Her whimsical decisions made her a difficult boss.

words.definition: to produce or provide (a result or crop); to give way to pressure or argument
words.nuance: Two common GRE senses: producing and giving in. Context decides.
examples: The experiment failed to yield any useful data.
The senator would not yield to pressure from party leaders.

words.definition: anxiety or fear that something bad will happen; understanding
words.nuance: The common sense is unease about the future; the rarer sense is grasping an idea.
examples: She waited for the test results with growing apprehension.
There is widespread apprehension about job losses.

words.definition: self-evident or unquestionable
words.nuance: Implies something accepted without needing proof.
examples: It is axiomatic that a good teacher must also be a good listener.
For the founders, the right to free speech was axiomatic.

words.definition: to come or bring to an end; to stop
words.nuance: Formal; often in 'cease to' or 'cease and desist'.
examples: The factory will cease production at the end of the year.
Both sides agreed to cease hostilities at midnight.

words.definition: making a certain situation or outcome likely or possible
words.nuance: Usually with 'to'; it describes conditions that help something happen.
examples: A quiet room is conducive to concentration.
The tense atmosphere was hardly conducive to compromise.

words.definition: relating to the body or the physical world rather than the spirit
words.nuance: Formal; contrasts the bodily with the spiritual.
examples: The mystics sought to escape their corporeal existence.
Ghosts in the story have no corporeal form.

words.definition: unreasonably high, especially of prices or demands
words.nuance: Critical; it implies going far beyond what is fair.
examples: Tourists complained about the exorbitant prices at the airport.
The landlord's exorbitant demands drove out his tenants.

words.definition: departing from the literal meaning; metaphorical
words.nuance: Contrasts with 'literal'; in art it means representing real forms.
examples: The phrase 'heart of stone' is figurative, not literal.
The poet's figurative language makes the landscape come alive.

words.definition: agitated or confused, especially from being rushed
words.nuance: Suggests flushed, temporary confusion rather than deep distress.
examples: The flustered waiter dropped a tray of glasses.
She was flustered by the unexpected question.

words.definition: easily persuaded to believe something; credulous
words.nuance: Critical; it implies that the person is easily fooled.
examples: Scammers target gullible investors with promises of quick profits.
Only a gullible reader would believe that headline.

words.definition: occurring as a minor accompaniment or by chance; not central
words.nuance: Stresses secondary importance.
examples: The film's incidental music was composed by a famous jazz pianist.
These details are incidental to the main argument.

words.definition: firmly fixed or established, difficult to change
words.nuance: Often of habits, attitudes or prejudices.
examples: Such deeply ingrained habits are hard to break.
The ingrained prejudice of the town shocked the newcomers.

words.definition: showing a rude and arrogant lack of respect
words.nuance: Stronger than 'rude'; it implies contempt for authority.
examples: The insolent student mocked the teacher openly.
His insolent reply cost him the promotion.

words.definition: sumptuously rich or elaborate; given in great amounts
words.nuance: As a verb, 'lavish praise on' means to give generously.
examples: The couple threw a lavish party for their anniversary.
Critics heaped lavish praise on the debut novel.

words.definition: looking or sounding sad and dismal, often exaggeratedly so
words.nuance: It can hint that the gloom is excessive or even comic.
examples: The comedian wore a lugubrious expression that made the audience laugh even harder.
The lugubrious music suited the funeral scene.

words.definition: disturbing because concerned with death or injury; gruesome
words.nuance: Stresses a grim fascination with death.
examples: The museum has a macabre collection of medieval torture devices.
He told the story with a macabre sense of humor.

words.definition: sullen and ill-tempered; gloomy
words.nuance: Implies bad temper and withdrawal, not just sadness.
examples: After the defeat, the team sat in morose silence.
He became morose and withdrawn in his final years.

words.definition: assertive of authority in an annoyingly domineering way, especially in petty matters
words.nuance: Not the same as 'official'; it criticizes unwanted interference.
examples: An officious clerk refused to stamp the form until every line was redone.
Her officious manner annoyed the volunteers.

words.definition: a complex or unwelcome consequence of an action or event
words.nuance: Implies consequences branching out in many directions.
examples: The most worrying ramification of the ruling concerns privacy law.
Consider every ramification before signing the deal.

words.definition: calm, peaceful and untroubled
words.nuance: Positive; it suggests deep tranquility rather than mere quiet.
examples: Her serene expression hid her nervousness.
The serene lake reflected the snowy peaks.

words.definition: to take the place of, often by force or by being better
words.nuance: Implies replacing something established.
examples: Streaming services threatened to supplant traditional television.
The general plotted to supplant the king.

words.definition: to go beyond the limits of something; to surpass
words.nuance: Often in an elevated sense, rising above ordinary limits.
examples: Great art can transcend cultural boundaries.
Their friendship was strong enough to transcend political differences.

words.definition: a formal, systematic written work on a subject
words.nuance: Implies a long and serious study, not a short article.
examples: Newton's treatise on optics influenced generations of scientists.
She published a lengthy treatise on Roman law.

words.definition: to cause someone to become hostile
words.nuance: Implies provoking hostility, often unnecessarily.
examples: The senator did not want to antagonize his own supporters.
Her blunt remarks managed to antagonize everyone in the room.

words.definition: too poor to produce vegetation; unproductive or lacking
words.nuance: Figuratively, it describes something empty of ideas or results.
examples: Nothing grew on the barren hillside.
The meeting proved barren of new ideas.

words.definition: to persuade someone by flattery or gentle urging
words.nuance: Gentle and persistent rather than forceful.
examples: She tried to cajole her brother into lending her the car.
The teacher had to cajole the shy students to speak.

words.definition: a bad-tempered, surly person, often old
words.nuance: Can be affectionate, describing a lovable grump.
examples: The neighborhood curmudgeon yelled at children who walked on his lawn.
Beneath his curmudgeon exterior was a generous heart.

words.definition: a mournful song or piece of music, especially for the dead
words.nuance: Figuratively, any slow, mournful sound.
examples: The band played a slow dirge as the coffin passed.
The wind's dirge through the pines kept her awake.

words.definition: worthy of great respect
words.nuance: Admiring and formal; not 'able to be estimated'.
examples: She was an estimable scholar whose work shaped the field.
His estimable record of public service earned him the award.

words.definition: a mild or indirect word substituted for one that is harsh or blunt
words.nuance: Neutral but often used critically for language that hides an unpleasant truth.
examples: 'Downsizing' is a euphemism for firing people.
He used a euphemism to avoid saying the word 'died'.

words.definition: pressing and demanding immediate attention; requiring much effort
words.nuance: Formal; it can describe urgent circumstances or demanding people.
examples: Police may enter without a warrant only in exigent circumstances.
The exigent demands of the job left her no time for hobbies.

words.definition: having a strong, exhilarating effect; intoxicating
words.nuance: Suggests excitement that can cloud judgment.
examples: Those were the heady days of the dot-com boom.
The perfume's heady scent filled the room.

words.definition: to criticize harshly
words.nuance: Emphatic and often public; stronger than 'criticize'.
examples: Reviewers were quick to lambaste the sequel as lazy and dull.
The editorial went on to lambaste the mayor for wasting funds.

words.definition: a person who behaves badly or breaks the law
words.nuance: Slightly old-fashioned and sometimes humorous.
examples: The police finally caught the miscreant who had been vandalizing cars.
Each miscreant in the class was sent to the principal's office.

words.definition: a small, relatively unimportant offense or sin
words.nuance: Mild and often indulgent; it minimizes the wrong.
examples: Voters forgave the senator's peccadillo but not his lies about it.
A peccadillo such as jaywalking hardly deserves a fine.

words.definition: a person who is hostile or indifferent to culture and the arts
words.nuance: Critical; it suggests narrow, materialistic tastes.
examples: Only a philistine would tear down the historic theater to build a parking lot.
He dismissed critics of his abstract paintings as philistine boors, though one philistine bought three.

words.definition: to assign to an inferior rank, position or condition
words.nuance: Implies being pushed aside or downgraded.
examples: The new manager tried to relegate the veteran to the bench.
Each new device seems to relegate its predecessor to a drawer.

words.definition: extremely distasteful; offensive
words.nuance: Strong; it implies moral or physical disgust.
examples: Most people find cruelty to animals repugnant.
The idea of lying under oath was repugnant to her.

words.definition: prompted by tender feelings of nostalgia or sadness, often excessively
words.nuance: Can be neutral ('sentimental value') or critical (cloying).
examples: The old watch has little monetary but great sentimental value.
Critics found the film's ending overly sentimental.

words.definition: to cheat someone out of money or possessions
words.nuance: Implies deliberate fraud.
examples: The con artist managed to swindle retirees out of their savings.
They planned to swindle the insurance company with a fake claim.

words.definition: perceptible by touch; clear and definite, real
words.nuance: Often used of results, evidence or benefits that are concrete.
examples: The reform produced few tangible benefits for ordinary workers.
There was a tangible sense of relief in the room.

words.definition: depravity; wickedness
words.nuance: Formal, often legal: 'moral turpitude'.
examples: The lawyer was disbarred for conduct involving moral turpitude.
The novel exposes the turpitude of the ruling class.

words.definition: complete and unreserved; (of metal) not mixed
words.nuance: Used of feelings such as joy or pleasure that are pure and unmixed.
examples: The victory brought unalloyed joy to the town.
The festival was an unalloyed success.

words.definition: to weaken or undermine; to offer goods at a lower price than a competitor
words.nuance: Two senses: weakening something, or selling cheaper.
examples: Discount retailers undercut local shops on price.
Her own data seemed to undercut her conclusion.

words.definition: to use flattery or coaxing to persuade someone
words.nuance: Implies sly, ingratiating persuasion.
examples: The children tried to wheedle a later bedtime out of their parents.
He would wheedle and flatter until he got his way.

words.definition: having an intense or irrational dislike or fear of people from other countries
words.nuance: Strongly negative.
examples: The candidate's xenophobic rhetoric alarmed immigrant communities.
Economic crises can stoke xenophobic sentiment.

words.definition: a state of temporary suspension or inactivity
words.nuance: Usually in 'in abeyance' or 'held in abeyance'.
examples: The plans were held in abeyance until the funding was approved.
The custom fell into abeyance after the war; its abeyance lasted decades.

words.definition: existing as an idea rather than as something physical or concrete; theoretical
words.nuance: As a noun, an abstract is a short summary of a study.
examples: Justice is an abstract concept that is hard to define.
Her arguments were too abstract to persuade the jury.

words.definition: an action or remark that causes outrage or offense
words.nuance: Implies an insult to dignity or values.
examples: The ruling was seen as an affront to free speech.
She took his refusal as a personal affront.

words.definition: to make someone troubled or nervous; to campaign to arouse public concern
words.nuance: Two senses: disturbing someone's calm, or stirring up support for a cause.
examples: Activists continued to agitate for voting rights.
The news seemed to agitate the patient.

words.definition: respected and impressive; dignified
words.nuance: Stress on the second syllable distinguishes it from the month.
examples: She was elected to the august body of the Royal Society.
The august halls of the university awed new students.

words.definition: to polish by rubbing; to enhance or improve (a reputation or image)
words.nuance: The figurative sense, polishing a reputation, is common in GRE passages.
examples: The candidate used the charity event to burnish her image.
Craftsmen burnish the silver until it gleams.

words.definition: pretending to be shy or modest; reluctant to give information
words.nuance: Often implies playful or evasive reluctance.
examples: The company remained coy about its plans for a new phone.
She gave a coy smile and changed the subject.

words.definition: to express disapproval of; to belittle
words.nuance: Self-deprecating humor belittles oneself; in tech, deprecated features are discouraged.
examples: It is unwise to deprecate the efforts of volunteers.
Critics deprecate the program as a waste of money.

words.definition: the feeling that someone or something is unworthy of respect
words.nuance: Stronger than dislike; it implies looking down on something.
examples: She regarded the tabloids with disdain.
His disdain for rules got him into trouble.

words.definition: to scatter or spread over a wide area; to break up
words.nuance: Used of crowds, light, seeds and information.
examples: Police used water cannons to disperse the crowd.
Wind helps the plant disperse its seeds.

words.definition: to swell or cause to swell by pressure from within
words.nuance: Physical and often medical.
examples: Starvation can cause the abdomen to distend.
The balloon began to distend as it filled with water.

words.definition: regularly found among a particular people or in a particular area; native
words.nuance: Often of diseases or problems that are built into a place or system.
examples: The koala is endemic to Australia.
Corruption was endemic in the old regime.

words.definition: the state of being actively opposed or hostile to someone
words.nuance: Deep, lasting hostility, often between groups.
examples: Years of enmity between the two families ended with a marriage.
Their political enmity was well known.

words.definition: lacking ease or grace; socially awkward
words.nuance: Borrowed from French for 'left'; it implies tactlessness.
examples: It would be gauche to discuss money at the wedding.
His gauche attempts at flattery embarrassed everyone.

words.definition: deriving from uncontrolled extreme emotion; extremely funny
words.nuance: Two senses: wildly emotional, or (informally) hilarious.
examples: The crowd's reaction bordered on the hysterical.
Some commentators called the warnings hysterical and overblown.

words.definition: not showing due respect; impertinent
words.nuance: Suggests cheeky boldness, often from a subordinate.
examples: The impudent child stuck out his tongue at the teacher.
She found the reporter's questions impudent.

words.definition: just begun and not fully formed; rudimentary
words.nuance: Formal; often of ideas or plans not yet developed.
examples: Her thoughts on the subject were still inchoate.
The inchoate movement lacked a leader.

words.definition: a strong liking or inclination for something
words.nuance: Lighter than 'propensity'; often for pleasures or quirks.
examples: She has a penchant for expensive shoes.
His penchant for exaggeration made his stories entertaining.

words.definition: a state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation
words.nuance: Implies being stuck between choices.
examples: The job offer put her in a quandary about leaving home.
Doctors often face an ethical quandary when resources are scarce.

words.definition: a state or period of isolation to prevent the spread of disease
words.nuance: As a verb, to isolate; figuratively, to cut off from contact.
examples: Travelers from the region were placed in quarantine for two weeks.
The ship remained under quarantine until the illness was identified.

words.definition: to reject or void, especially by legal procedure; to put an end to
words.nuance: Suggests firmly crushing a rumor, rebellion or ruling.
examples: The appeals court voted to quash the conviction.
The company moved quickly to quash rumors of a sale.

words.definition: to argue or raise objections about a trivial matter
words.nuance: Suggests petty, minor objections.
examples: They tend to quibble over the wording of every sentence.
There is no point to quibble about a few cents.

words.definition: to cause severe and extensive damage to
words.nuance: Implies violent, widespread destruction.
examples: Wildfires continue to ravage the dry forests each summer.
Disease would ravage the city's population within months.

words.definition: to say that one no longer holds an opinion or belief, especially publicly
words.nuance: Implies a formal, often forced, withdrawal.
examples: Under pressure, the witness agreed to recant her testimony.
Galileo was forced to recant his views on the solar system.

words.definition: formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of respect
words.nuance: Admiring; it suggests a person to be feared or respected.
examples: She was a redoubtable debater who rarely lost.
The redoubtable general had never been defeated.

words.definition: tending to avoid company; shy
words.nuance: Not about leaving a job; it describes a shy temperament.
examples: Despite her fame, she remained a retiring person who avoided parties.
His retiring nature made public speaking an ordeal.

words.definition: high-pitched and piercing; (of a complaint) loud and forceful
words.nuance: Figuratively, used critically of strident protests.
examples: A shrill whistle signaled the end of the shift.
Critics dismissed the campaign as shrill and alarmist.

words.definition: skilled at gaining an advantage, especially deceitfully
words.nuance: Suggests clever, crafty scheming.
examples: The wily politician survived every scandal.
Even the wily fox could not escape the trap.

words.definition: to leave hurriedly and secretly, typically to avoid arrest or with stolen goods
words.nuance: Implies secret flight, often with something that isn't one's own.
examples: The treasurer tried to abscond with the club's funds.
Several prisoners managed to abscond from the work camp.

words.definition: an attack on the reputation or integrity of someone
words.nuance: Usually in 'cast aspersions on'.
examples: I am not trying to cast an aspersion on your honesty.
The article contained one aspersion after another against the mayor.

words.definition: dealing with sexual matters in a comical way; humorously indecent
words.nuance: Lighthearted rather than obscene.
examples: The tavern rang with bawdy songs.
Chaucer's bawdy tales still amuse readers.

words.definition: distress or embarrassment at having failed or been humiliated
words.nuance: Often in 'to one's chagrin'; it mixes annoyance with embarrassment.
examples: Much to his chagrin, his younger brother beat him at chess.
The team's loss was a source of chagrin for its loyal fans.

words.definition: to cooperate secretly or illegally to deceive or cheat others
words.nuance: Negative; often of companies fixing prices or officials conspiring.
examples: Regulators say the companies agreed to collude on prices.
Officials who collude with smugglers undermine border security.

words.definition: to express sympathy or sorrow with someone
words.nuance: Implies sharing in another's disappointment.
examples: Fans gathered at the bar to commiserate after the defeat.
She called to commiserate with her friend about the lost job.

words.definition: an extensive, destructive fire; a large-scale conflict
words.nuance: Figuratively used of wars.
examples: The conflagration destroyed most of the old city.
Diplomats feared the border clash could spark a wider conflagration.

words.definition: a minor dispute or disagreement; an unfortunate occurrence
words.nuance: Mild; it suggests a small, embarrassing clash.
examples: A contretemps over seating nearly ruined the dinner.
The diplomatic contretemps was resolved with an apology.

words.definition: a firmly held belief; the quality of showing that one is sure of something
words.nuance: Also a legal term, a guilty verdict; on the GRE, usually firm belief.
examples: She spoke with such conviction that the audience believed her.
His religious conviction guided every decision he made.

words.definition: to sing or hum in a soft, low voice, especially sentimentally
words.nuance: Suggests gentle, intimate singing.
examples: She would croon lullabies until the baby fell asleep.
The singer began to croon an old ballad.

words.definition: to remove from office suddenly and forcefully; to testify under oath
words.nuance: The political sense, ousting a ruler, is most common.
examples: The army moved to depose the president in a bloodless coup.
Lawyers will depose the witness next week.

words.definition: the easing of hostility or strained relations, especially between countries
words.nuance: Strongly associated with Cold War diplomacy.
examples: The summit marked a period of detente between the rival powers.
A fragile detente settled over the two feuding departments.

words.definition: unfashionable and without style in appearance
words.nuance: Mildly unkind; usually about clothes or appearance.
examples: The brand tried to shed its dowdy image with a new campaign.
She felt dowdy next to her glamorous cousin.

words.definition: a level or rank in an organization, profession or society
words.nuance: Usually in 'upper echelons'.
examples: She rose to the highest echelon of the company.
Only the top echelon of officials knew the plan.

words.definition: a feeling of listlessness and dissatisfaction arising from boredom
words.nuance: Literary; suggests a weary, almost existential boredom.
examples: The novel captures the ennui of life in a small town.
A deep ennui settled over him during the long winter.

words.definition: to speak or write at length or in detail
words.nuance: Formal; usually with 'on' or 'upon'.
examples: The professor would expatiate on Roman history for hours.
He liked to expatiate upon the virtues of his hometown.

words.definition: filled with something undesirable; causing or feeling anxiety
words.nuance: Usually 'fraught with danger, difficulty or tension'.
examples: The journey across the mountains was fraught with danger.
Relations between the two nations remain fraught.

words.definition: the point on which a lever turns; a thing that plays a central role in an activity
words.nuance: The figurative sense is a pivotal element.
examples: The midfielder was the fulcrum of the team's attack.
Trade became the fulcrum of the region's economy.

words.definition: an extremely confused, complicated or embarrassing situation
words.nuance: Suggests a tangled scandal or dispute.
examples: The minister was caught up in a political imbroglio over the contracts.
The family imbroglio over the will dragged on for years.

words.definition: cheerful and lighthearted
words.nuance: Literary.
examples: The jocund host kept everyone laughing.
Her jocund spirit lifted the gloomy office.

words.definition: to lose or lack vitality; to suffer from being forced to remain in an unpleasant place
words.nuance: Implies wasting away from neglect or confinement.
examples: The bill was left to languish in committee.
He continued to languish in prison while his case was appealed.

words.definition: quick and light in movement; quick to understand
words.nuance: Positive, of bodies or minds.
examples: The nimble goat leapt from rock to rock.
A nimble mind can see solutions others miss.

words.definition: giving the impression that something bad is going to happen
words.nuance: Suggests a threatening sign or atmosphere.
examples: Ominous clouds gathered over the hills.
There was an ominous silence after the announcement.

words.definition: looking or sounding bizarre or unfamiliar
words.nuance: Suggests strangeness that strains belief.
examples: The tabloid made outlandish claims about the singer.
He showed up in an outlandish costume of feathers and foil.

words.definition: having or encouraging an excessive interest in sexual matters
words.nuance: Disapproving.
examples: The tabloid catered to readers' prurient interest in celebrity scandals.
Critics accused the film of prurient sensationalism.

words.definition: deriving pleasure from inflicting pain or humiliation on others
words.nuance: Strongly negative.
examples: The sadistic guard enjoyed tormenting prisoners.
The exam seemed designed by a sadistic professor.

words.definition: departing from an accepted standard; abnormal
words.nuance: Often clinical; it describes behavior or results that are not typical.
examples: The scientist discarded the aberrant data point.
His aberrant behavior worried his teachers.

words.definition: to accept or tolerate (usually in the negative); to act in accordance with (a rule)
words.nuance: 'Can't abide' means can't stand; 'abide by' means obey.
examples: I cannot abide people who talk during films.
All members must abide by the club's rules.

words.definition: a bold manner intended to impress or intimidate, often masking fear
words.nuance: Critical; it implies show rather than real courage.
examples: His bravado vanished the moment the plane hit turbulence.
Beneath the bravado, he was terrified.

words.definition: to think deeply about something; to meditate
words.nuance: Formal and sometimes humorous.
examples: She paused to cogitate on the offer before replying.
Philosophers cogitate about questions others never ask.

words.definition: the way a person behaves, especially their bearing and manners
words.nuance: Old-fashioned; it suggests polished conduct.
examples: Finishing schools once taught young women deportment.
His deportment at court was always correct.

words.definition: to speak or perform without preparation
words.nuance: Implies improvising when something unexpected happens.
examples: When the slides failed, she had to extemporize for twenty minutes.
Jazz musicians extemporize around a familiar melody.

words.definition: relating to or inclined to dissension; divided into factions
words.nuance: Not 'factual' or 'fractious', though close to the latter in spirit.
examples: The factious party could not agree on a leader.
Factious disputes paralyzed the committee.

words.definition: (of land) left unplanted; inactive or unproductive for a period
words.nuance: Figuratively, a fallow period is a time of rest before new productivity.
examples: Farmers let the field lie fallow for a season.
After a fallow decade, the writer published three novels.

words.definition: a deceptive movement intended to distract an opponent
words.nuance: Used in sports, fencing and military tactics.
examples: The boxer threw a feint before landing his punch.
The army's attack in the north was only a feint.

words.definition: conspicuously or obviously offensive
words.nuance: Implies wrongdoing that is shamelessly open.
examples: The referee called a flagrant foul.
The report described a flagrant disregard for safety rules.

words.definition: to act obsequiously to obtain forgiveness or favor
words.nuance: Contemptuous; it implies humiliating self-abasement.
examples: He refused to grovel before the board.
She had to grovel to get her old job back.

words.definition: not in keeping with good taste and propriety; improper
words.nuance: Formal.
examples: Laughing loudly at the funeral seemed indecorous.
The sale of the estate proceeded with indecorous haste.

words.definition: to arouse the curiosity or interest of; to plot secretly
words.nuance: As a noun it means secret plotting.
examples: The mystery of the lost city continues to intrigue historians.
The court was full of intrigue and betrayal.

words.definition: existing in name only; (of a price) very small
words.nuance: Two senses: in name only, and token in amount.
examples: The queen is the nominal head of state but has little power.
Members pay only a nominal fee.

words.definition: noisy and difficult to control
words.nuance: Suggests loud resistance.
examples: The obstreperous fans were escorted out of the stadium.
An obstreperous toddler can wear out any parent.

words.definition: extremely unpleasant; repulsive
words.nuance: Strong; it implies hatefulness.
examples: Cleaning the sewer was an odious task.
He found the regime's policies odious.

words.definition: having or showing determined courage in the face of difficulties
words.nuance: Affectionate; often used of underdogs.
examples: The plucky underdog team reached the final.
A plucky reporter refused to drop the story.

words.definition: money paid for work or a service
words.nuance: Formal; not 'renumeration'.
examples: The remuneration for the job was surprisingly low.
Executives received generous remuneration despite the losses.

words.definition: messy and careless in appearance or work
words.nuance: Critical.
examples: His slovenly appearance did not impress the interviewers.
The report was full of slovenly errors.

words.definition: a speech in which a character speaks their thoughts aloud, alone on stage
words.nuance: A dramatic term; also any long talk to oneself.
examples: Hamlet's soliloquy reveals his doubts about revenge.
The actor delivered the soliloquy in a hushed voice.

words.definition: to reject with disdain or contempt
words.nuance: Stronger than 'reject'; it implies scorn.
examples: She chose to spurn his offer of help.
It is unwise to spurn advice from those who have done the job before.

words.definition: very weak or slight; insubstantial
words.nuance: Often of connections, arguments or holds on power.
examples: The link between the two events is tenuous at best.
The government has a tenuous hold on power.

words.definition: vigor and spirit or enthusiasm
words.nuance: Positive; suggests lively style.
examples: The orchestra played the overture with great verve.
Her writing has a verve that keeps readers hooked.

words.definition: to repeal or formally do away with a law, right or agreement
words.nuance: Formal and legal; it implies official cancellation.
examples: The new government moved to abrogate the trade treaty.
No court may abrogate the rights guaranteed by the constitution.

words.definition: filled with horror or shock
words.nuance: Strong; often 'aghast at'.
examples: Parents were aghast at the new school policy.
She stared, aghast, at the wreckage.

words.definition: to inform or tell someone
words.nuance: Formal; usually 'apprise someone of something'.
examples: Please apprise me of any changes to the schedule.
The lawyer will apprise the client of her rights.

words.definition: to charm or enchant, sometimes in a deceptive way
words.nuance: Can be positive (charm) or negative (trick).
examples: The story will beguile readers of all ages.
He tried to beguile the investors with false promises.

words.definition: a thing that is helpful or beneficial
words.nuance: Positive; often 'a boon to' or 'a boon for'.
examples: The new railway was a boon to local farmers.
Remote work has been a boon for parents.

words.definition: showing or having an insensitive and cruel disregard for others
words.nuance: Strongly critical; the noun 'callus' is hardened skin.
examples: The landlord's callous disregard for his tenants shocked the court.
It was a callous remark to make at a funeral.

words.definition: to treat someone in an overprotective or indulgent way
words.nuance: Critical; it implies spoiling.
examples: Critics say schools coddle students instead of challenging them.
She refused to coddle her players after a loss.

words.definition: a gradual increase in loudness or intensity; the most intense point
words.nuance: Strictly the build-up, but often used for the climax.
examples: The music swelled to a crescendo.
Complaints rose to a crescendo before the minister resigned.

words.definition: (of circumstances) serving to make a fault seem less serious
words.nuance: Usually in 'extenuating circumstances'.
examples: The judge reduced the sentence because of extenuating circumstances.
There were no extenuating factors to excuse the delay.

words.definition: fast and energetic in a wild or uncontrolled way
words.nuance: Suggests frantic activity.
examples: The city moves at a frenetic pace.
There was frenetic activity in the newsroom on election night.

words.definition: not part of the mainstream; peripheral or extreme
words.nuance: As a noun, the outer edge of an area or group.
examples: Only a fringe group supported the extreme proposal.
The idea began as a fringe theory before winning acceptance.

words.definition: unfortunate
words.nuance: Sympathetic or mildly mocking.
examples: The hapless tourist lost his wallet on the first day.
The hapless team lost its tenth straight game.

words.definition: perfectly clean, neat or tidy; free from flaws
words.nuance: Stresses spotless perfection.
examples: The vintage car was in immaculate condition.
She kept an immaculate record of every expense.

words.definition: to become rigid or fixed in attitude; to turn into bone
words.nuance: The figurative sense, institutions or ideas hardening, is common.
examples: Without new ideas, the party began to ossify.
Traditions can ossify into empty rituals.

words.definition: an artistic work that imitates the style of another work or period
words.nuance: Can be affectionate homage or a derivative jumble.
examples: The novel is a clever pastiche of Victorian detective stories.
The building's design is a pastiche of several historical styles.

words.definition: slow and clumsy because of great weight; dull and laborious
words.nuance: Of style, it means heavy and tedious.
examples: The ponderous elephant moved slowly through the grass.
His ponderous prose made the book hard to finish.

words.definition: a person who lives a solitary life and avoids other people
words.nuance: Neutral to sympathetic.
examples: The author became a recluse after her first novel.
The old recluse rarely left his cabin.

words.definition: to make an attack in return for a similar attack
words.nuance: Implies striking back.
examples: The country threatened to retaliate against the new tariffs.
When teased, he would retaliate with sarcasm.

words.definition: an effusively enthusiastic expression of feeling; a free-form piece of music
words.nuance: 'Rhapsodize' means to speak with great enthusiasm.
examples: The critic's review was a rhapsody of praise.
Gershwin's rhapsody blends jazz and classical music.

words.definition: occurring by happy chance
words.nuance: Positive; it implies a lucky accident.
examples: Penicillin was a serendipitous discovery.
Their meeting at the airport was serendipitous.

words.definition: to avoid or neglect a duty or responsibility
words.nuance: Critical.
examples: A good leader does not shirk responsibility for mistakes.
He was fired for trying to shirk his duties.

words.definition: a position requiring little or no work but giving status or pay
words.nuance: Critical; it implies an undeserved, cushy post.
examples: The job was a sinecure created for the mayor's nephew.
He spent his last years in a comfortable sinecure at the ministry.

words.definition: having many curves and turns; moving with graceful, curving motions
words.nuance: Often of rivers, roads and dancers.
examples: The sinuous river wound through the valley.
The dancer's sinuous movements captivated the audience.

words.definition: involving immoral or dishonorable actions; dirty or squalid
words.nuance: Implies moral or physical filth.
examples: The trial revealed the sordid details of the bribery scheme.
They lived in a sordid apartment above the bar.

words.definition: to stop or restrict a flow of blood or something else
words.nuance: Often figurative: to stanch losses.
examples: The medic struggled to stanch the bleeding.
The company cut prices to stanch its loss of customers.

words.definition: existing beyond what is obvious or admitted; intentionally hidden
words.nuance: Almost always in 'ulterior motive'.
examples: She suspected his kindness had an ulterior motive.
The plan's ulterior purpose was to drive out competitors.

words.definition: providing supplementary or additional help and support
words.nuance: Neutral; implies a backup role.
examples: The hospital switched to auxiliary power during the blackout.
Auxiliary staff helped run the conference.

words.definition: a picture or description in which features are exaggerated for comic or grotesque effect
words.nuance: Implies distortion, often mocking.
examples: The film presents a caricature of rural life.
The artist drew a caricature of the president with enormous ears.

words.definition: moral corruption; wickedness
words.nuance: Strong; implies deep moral decay.
examples: The novel explores the depravity of the criminal underworld.
Investigators were shocked by the depravity of the crimes.

words.definition: insolent or impertinent behavior; shameless boldness
words.nuance: Implies breathtaking nerve.
examples: He had the effrontery to ask for a raise after missing a month of work.
Her effrontery shocked the board.

words.definition: to intrude gradually on someone's territory, rights or time
words.nuance: Implies slow, creeping intrusion.
examples: New housing continues to encroach on the forest.
The new law may encroach upon civil liberties.

words.definition: to give or bequeath an income or property; to provide with a quality or ability
words.nuance: Common in 'endowed with talent'.
examples: The alumnus agreed to endow a new chair in philosophy.
Nature seemed to endow her with remarkable patience.

words.definition: to ask someone earnestly or anxiously to do something
words.nuance: Implies urgent, emotional pleading.
examples: She would entreat her father to let her travel alone.
The villagers entreat the king for mercy.

words.definition: a formal charge of a serious crime; a thing that shows something is bad and deserves condemnation
words.nuance: The figurative sense is common: 'an indictment of the system'.
examples: The report is a damning indictment of the prison system.
The grand jury handed down an indictment against the mayor.

words.definition: feeling or showing anger at something seen as unfair
words.nuance: Implies righteous anger.
examples: She was indignant at the suggestion that she had cheated.
Indignant residents packed the council meeting.

words.definition: unable to be resisted or avoided; inescapable
words.nuance: Formal and literary.
examples: The play moves toward its ineluctable tragic ending.
Aging is an ineluctable part of life.

words.definition: curious or inquiring; unduly curious about others' affairs
words.nuance: Usually positive for children and minds, negative for nosy neighbors.
examples: The inquisitive child asked endless questions.
An inquisitive neighbor peered over the fence.

words.definition: scope for freedom of action or thought
words.nuance: On the GRE, the freedom sense, not the geographic one.
examples: Teachers have considerable latitude in how they design lessons.
The judge allowed the lawyer some latitude in questioning.

words.definition: humor or frivolity, especially treating a serious matter with lack of respect
words.nuance: Can be welcome relief or inappropriate.
examples: His joke provided a moment of levity during the tense meeting.
The judge would not tolerate levity in the courtroom.

words.definition: having or showing a wish to do evil to others
words.nuance: Strongly negative; the opposite of benevolent.
examples: The villain's malevolent grin sent chills down my spine.
Some believed a malevolent spirit haunted the house.

words.definition: to intervene between people in a dispute in order to bring about an agreement
words.nuance: Neutral; implies an impartial go-between.
examples: A retired judge was asked to mediate the dispute.
The diplomat helped mediate between the warring factions.

words.definition: to stop, close up or obstruct
words.nuance: Formal and often medical.
examples: A blood clot can occlude an artery.
Tall buildings occlude the view of the bay.

words.definition: to quell the anger or agitation of; to bring peace to a place
words.nuance: Can also mean to subdue a region by force.
examples: The manager tried to pacify the angry customers.
Troops were sent to pacify the rebellious province.

words.definition: to treat with apparent kindness that betrays a feeling of superiority; to be a customer of
words.nuance: Two senses: condescend, or support as a customer.
examples: Please don't patronize me; I understand the risks.
Locals patronize the bakery every morning.

words.definition: having a pleasantly sharp taste; agreeably stimulating or provocative
words.nuance: Of food, spicy; of ideas or stories, intriguing.
examples: The piquant sauce gave the fish a lively kick.
Her memoir is full of piquant anecdotes about famous friends.

words.definition: flourishing or spreading unchecked
words.nuance: Negative; usually of disease, crime or corruption.
examples: Rampant inflation wiped out people's savings.
Rumors ran rampant through the office.

words.definition: (of a possibility) unlikely; aloof and distant in manner; far away
words.nuance: On the GRE, 'remote' often means slight, as in 'a remote chance', or aloof.
examples: There is only a remote chance of rain today.
His remote manner made him hard to befriend.

words.definition: an unprincipled person
words.nuance: Often humorous; suggests a lovable rogue.
examples: Her uncle was a charming old reprobate who never paid his debts.
The reprobate was finally banned from the casino.

words.definition: (of a liquid) cloudy or muddy; confused or disordered
words.nuance: Not 'turgid', which means swollen or pompous.
examples: Spring floods made the river turbid and brown.
The essay's turbid argument left readers confused.

words.definition: having or showing a lack of thought or intelligence; empty
words.nuance: Critical.
examples: The interview was full of vacuous remarks.
He gave a vacuous smile and said nothing.
